slides.title: Marine biology: life in the planet's largest habitat
slides.body:
**Marine biology**: the study of organisms in seawater + their interactions with the physical-chemical ocean. The ocean covers 71% of Earth + holds ~99% of habitable volume; marine ecosystems generate ~50% of atmospheric O₂ (via phytoplankton + cyanobacteria) + absorb ~25% of anthropogenic CO₂. Distinct from but overlapping with **oceanography** (the physical-chemical ocean) — marine biologists need both because organisms are shaped by, and shape, water column structure.

**Major depth zones**:
- **Epipelagic / euphotic** (0-200m): sunlit; phytoplankton + most fisheries; warm + variable.
- **Mesopelagic / 'twilight'** (200-1000m): dim light; bioluminescence prevalent; diel vertical migration (DVM) — largest daily animal migration on Earth.
- **Bathypelagic** (1000-4000m): no light; cold (~4°C); high pressure; sparse fauna with bizarre adaptations.
- **Abyssopelagic** (4000-6000m): deep-sea plains; manganese nodules; chemosynthetic vent communities.
- **Hadalpelagic** (>6000m): trenches (Marianas 11km); extremophiles.

**Coastal + benthic habitats**:
- **Intertidal**: tides; zonation (barnacles → mussels → algae → corallines).
- **Estuaries + mangroves**: brackish; nursery for many fish; high productivity.
- **Coral reefs**: tropical; symbiosis with zooxanthellae; biodiversity hotspots.
- **Kelp forests + seagrass**: temperate productivity hotspots.
- **Hydrothermal vents** (Alvin 1977 discovery): chemosynthesis-based; reshaped views of life.
- **Cold seeps**: methane hydrate communities.
- **Sea ice + polar seas**: ice algae + krill + whales.

**Why now matters**: climate change + acidification + overfishing + plastic pollution + deep-sea mining + offshore wind + aquaculture make marine biology one of the most urgent applied life sciences.

slides.title: Diversity + classification: from microbes to whales
slides.body:
**Marine life spans every major branch of the tree of life**. Most ocean biomass is microbial.

**Microbes + plankton**:
- **Bacteria + archaea** (~10²⁹ cells in oceans): heterotrophs + autotrophs + chemoautotrophs.
- **Phytoplankton** (cyanobacteria + diatoms + dinoflagellates + coccolithophores + haptophytes): half of global primary production.
- **Zooplankton** (copepods + krill + larvaceans + jellyfish + chaetognaths): graze + repackage carbon.
- **Virioplankton**: viruses, ~10⁷/mL; viral shunt recycles ~25% of fixed carbon.

**Invertebrates** (>95% of marine animals):
- Sponges, cnidarians (corals, jellyfish, sea anemones, hydroids).
- Comb jellies (ctenophores).
- Mollusks (bivalves, gastropods, cephalopods — octopuses are highly intelligent invertebrates).
- Crustaceans (copepods, krill, decapods).
- Echinoderms (sea stars, urchins, cucumbers).
- Polychaete + sipunculan worms.
- Tunicates / urochordates (closest invertebrate sister to vertebrates).

**Vertebrates**:
- Fishes (~33000 species): teleosts, elasmobranchs (sharks + rays), agnathans.
- Reptiles (sea turtles, sea snakes).
- Birds (penguins, seabirds — albatrosses with 3.5m wingspans).
- Marine mammals (cetaceans — whales + dolphins; pinnipeds — seals + walruses; sirenians — manatees + dugongs; mustelids — sea otters).

**Plants + algae**: kelp + seagrass + mangroves + green/red/brown macroalgae. Note: kelp + most 'seaweed' are protists (chromists), not plants.

**Biological classification + DNA barcoding** (COI gene + 18S rRNA) revolutionized marine taxonomy — many morphologically identical species are genetically distinct. Census of Marine Life (2000-2010) catalogued ~250000 known + ~750000 still-undescribed species.

slides.title: Marine biology as a science: methods + frontier
slides.body:
**Classic methods**:
- **Net + trawl sampling**: Plankton (Niskin bottles, CTD-rosette, Bongo nets, MOCNESS); trawls (otter trawl, mid-water IKMT).
- **Diving + ROV / AUV**: SCUBA to ~30m; technical to ~150m; submersibles (Alvin); ROVs (Jason, ROPOS); AUVs (Sentry, ABE).
- **Tagging + telemetry**: archival tags (TDRs), satellite tags (Argos, Wildlife Computers), acoustic (VEMCO).
- **Mark-recapture + photo-ID** (whale flukes, manta-ray spots).
- **Acoustic monitoring**: passive (PAM for cetaceans), active (echo sounders for fish biomass).
- **Microscopy + culture + flow cytometry** (microbial).
- **Ship-based + ocean-time-series stations**: BATS, HOT, CalCOFI, K2.

**Modern frontier**:
- **Environmental DNA (eDNA)**: detect species from filtered seawater; revolutionary for biodiversity surveys.
- **Omics**: metagenomics + metatranscriptomics + metabolomics on entire microbial communities. Tara Oceans + Malaspina expeditions sampled the global microbiome.
- **Argo float array** (>4000 free-drifting profilers measuring T+S+O₂+chl); BGC-Argo adds biology.
- **Satellite remote sensing**: chlorophyll (SeaWiFS, MODIS, VIIRS, OC-PACE), SST, sea level, ice cover, surface salinity (SMAP).
- **AI + computer vision**: automated species ID from images + audio (whale calls, fish counts).
- **Animal-borne biologgers**: cameras + ecology sensors on tags.
- **Genomics + CRISPR**: functional studies of marine organisms.
- **High-throughput sequencing**: viral discovery, microbial dark matter.

**Big science programs**: Census of Marine Life; GEOTRACES (trace metals); Tara Oceans (microbial); GOMECC (acidification); GO-SHIP (deep-water repeat hydrography); NEPTUNE/OOI cabled observatories; OCEAN VITAL (UN Decade).

question.question: Estimate global phytoplankton primary production
question.goal: Use ocean surface area + average chlorophyll-based productivity to estimate global net primary production (NPP) by phytoplankton.

steps.prompt: Typical satellite-derived NPP (g C / m² / yr)?
hints: Behrenfeld VGPM ~120-150 g C/m²/yr global avg.
steps.reveal: Global average ~130 g C / m² / yr (VGPM, CbPM models). High in coastal upwelling (~600); low in oligotrophic gyres (~50).

steps.prompt: Global ocean NPP in Pg C / yr?
steps.reveal: Global ocean NPP ≈ 3.6 × 10¹⁴ m² × 130 g C/m²/yr ≈ 47 × 10¹⁵ g C/yr ≈ 47 Pg C/yr. Roughly half of global NPP (terrestrial ~55 Pg C/yr); accomplished by ~1% of plant biomass on Earth due to phytoplankton's rapid turnover (days).

steps.prompt: What fraction of this fuels the biological carbon pump (BCP)?
steps.reveal: ~10% of NPP exports below the mixed layer (the 'biological carbon pump'); ~1-2% reaches the deep sea + sequesters carbon on millennial timescales. The pump removes ~5-12 Pg C/yr from atmosphere; without it atmospheric CO₂ would be ~200 ppm higher.

question.question: Why does the ocean produce ~50% of Earth's photosynthetic oxygen with only ~1% of plant biomass?
options: Phytoplankton turn over in days (vs months/years for terrestrial plants); biomass at any instant is tiny but flux through it is enormous. Per-area productivity is comparable to land; the ocean's huge surface area (71%) + rapid turnover give it ~50% of NPP. Phytoplankton (cyanobacteria, diatoms, coccolithophores, dinoflagellates, haptophytes) fix carbon while predators (zooplankton) immediately graze + recycle nutrients — the 'microbial loop' + 'biological pump' operate fast.
question.explanation: Standing biomass vs flux distinction is the key insight. Phytoplankton biomass turns over in ~1-10 days; terrestrial forest biomass turns over in decades. Per-area productivity is comparable but ocean covers 71% of surface so total NPP is roughly half of global. Foundation of marine biogeochemistry + ecosystem modeling.

slides.workedSolution: Phytoplankton turn over in days vs years for land plants; standing biomass is low but flux through it is high. Ocean's large area (71%) + fast turnover give it ~50% of global NPP. Foundation of biogeochemistry + carbon-cycle modeling.

question.question: Classify each organism by its ocean zone or habitat.
question.explanation: Vertical + latitudinal zonation: epipelagic (sun, phytoplankton, big fish, top predators); mesopelagic (twilight, bioluminescence, diel migration); deep benthic + vents (chemosynthesis); polar ice (ice algae + krill + dependents). Zoning shapes ecology + fisheries + climate sensitivity.

question.question: Drag to approximate fraction (%) of Earth's surface covered by ocean.
question.explanation: Ocean covers ~71% of Earth's surface (~361 million km² out of 510 million km²). Pacific + Atlantic + Indian + Arctic + Southern oceans. Average depth ~3700m; deepest point Marianas Trench ~10984m (Challenger Deep).

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why marine biology is one of the most consequential applied life sciences today.
question.rubric: Mentions: ocean covers 71% of Earth + holds 99% of habitable volume + drives climate (heat + CO₂ sequestration ~25% of anthropogenic CO₂; ~50% of O₂ from phytoplankton). Anthropogenic pressures: overfishing (1/3 of global fisheries overexploited), warming (marine heatwaves + coral bleaching), acidification (~0.1 pH unit drop since 1750), deoxygenation (OMZ expansion), plastic pollution (Great Pacific Garbage Patch), eutrophication + harmful algal blooms, sea-level rise affecting coastal ecosystems, deep-sea mining of polymetallic nodules + sulfides, offshore wind + tidal energy, aquaculture (now > capture fisheries by tonnage). Tools to monitor + respond exist now (eDNA, Argo, satellite, omics, AI). The UN Decade of Ocean Science (2021-2030) is an unprecedented coordinated push. Concludes: marine biology now sits at the intersection of climate, food security, biodiversity loss, and emerging blue economy.
